**ARGUMENT**

**The Proposed Class Cannot Be Certified Under Rule 23(b)(3) Because Individualized Damages Questions Will Overwhelm Any Common Questions.**

**A. Plaintiff must prove predominance with evidence.**

Plaintiff bears the burden of proving each disputed Rule 23 requirement by a preponderance of the evidence. *Messner v. Northshore Univ. HealthSystem*, 669 F.3d 802, 811 (7th Cir. 2012). The Court need not accept the complaint's allegations as true. It must make the factual and legal inquiries that certification requires, even when they overlap with the merits. *Szabo v. Bridgeport Machs., Inc.*, 249 F.3d 672, 675–77 (7th Cir. 2001). And where expert testimony is critical to certification, the Court must resolve any challenge to its reliability before certifying a class. *Am. Honda Motor Co. v. Allen*, 600 F.3d 813, 815–16 (7th Cir. 2010). A promise that a workable damages method will emerge later does not carry Plaintiff's burden.

Rule 23(b)(3) requires that common questions predominate over individual ones. A question is individual when class members must present evidence that varies from member to member; it is common when the same evidence will suffice for each. *Messner*, 669 F.3d at 815.

**B. Plaintiff must offer a realistic classwide damages method tied to the theory of liability.**

A damages model must measure only the damages attributable to the theory of liability the class pursues. *Comcast Corp. v. Behrend*, 569 U.S. 27, 35 (2013). Without such a model, individual damages calculations will inevitably overwhelm common questions. *Id.* at 34. The Seventh Circuit enforces that requirement. In *Parko v. Shell Oil Co.*, property owners alleged that contamination from a refinery had reduced their property values. The court vacated certification because the district court had not tested the realism of the plaintiffs' injury and damages model against the defendants' counterarguments. 739 F.3d 1083, 1085–86 (7th Cir. 2014).

Plaintiff here has not made that showing. Each class member's recovery turns on [identify member-specific variables, e.g., amount paid, usage, exposure, mitigation, offsets, and alternative causes]. [Describe Plaintiff's proposed model, or its absence, and why it cannot isolate losses caused by the challenged conduct.]

**C. Individualized damages proceedings would swamp this litigation.**

*Espenscheid v. DirectSat USA, LLC*, 705 F.3d 770 (7th Cir. 2013), is instructive. There, the Seventh Circuit affirmed decertification of Rule 23 classes and an FLSA collective action involving some 2,341 technicians whose unpaid time varied. *Id.* at 772–73. Determining damages threatened to require thousands of separate evidentiary hearings, and the plaintiffs had not shown that testimony from a small set of hand-picked "representative" members could reliably establish what everyone else was owed. *Id.* at 773–76. They also failed to propose a feasible litigation plan. *Id.* at 775–76.

The same problem exists here. [State the number of class members and the evidence each damages determination would require.] Averaging or sampling cannot erase those differences unless the sample is shown to be representative. *See id.* at 774–76. Nor may a class be certified on the premise that [Defendant] will lose its right to litigate defenses to individual claims. *Wal-Mart Stores, Inc. v. Dukes*, 564 U.S. 338, 367 (2011). Where liability itself also depends on individual circumstances, predominance is lacking all the more clearly. *See Harper v. Sheriff of Cook Cnty.*, 581 F.3d 511, 513–16 (7th Cir. 2009) (reversing certification where individualized inquiries predominated).

**D. Bifurcation does not cure the defect.**

[Defendant] recognizes that individual damages questions do not by themselves automatically defeat certification. *Messner*, 669 F.3d at 815. A court may, in an appropriate case, certify liability issues and leave damages to separate proceedings. *Butler v. Sears, Roebuck & Co.*, 727 F.3d 796, 800–01 (7th Cir. 2013). But that approach is useful only when a common liability judgment would materially advance the litigation and the remaining proceedings are manageable. Here, [explain why injury, causation, and amount are intertwined, so that a liability phase would resolve little and each follow-on proceeding would revisit the same evidence]. Deferring those questions would postpone the individualized trials, not eliminate them. Certification should be denied.
